source.title: Towards Principled Design of Mixture-of-Experts Language Models under Memory and Inference Constraints
source.authors: Seng Pei Liew; K. Shinzato; Yu-Yang Dong

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling-law relationships and architecture choices in Mixture-of-Experts language models, an extension of the cited dense-language-model scaling work to MoE models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out-loss results from MoE architecture ablations, scaling-law fits, and a comparison of two MoE configurations across model and dataset sizes. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains Qwen3-like MoE language models on FineWeb-Edu and measures held-out loss. It fits power laws in total parameters (30M–3B at 9B tokens) and Chinchilla-style N,D laws for two configurations (9B–50B tokens), and ablates granularity and width-to-depth at roughly fixed total and active parameters. Its own results bear on V1, V4 and V7 in a new setting (sparse MoE) that the original sources did not cover.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MoE loss is driven mainly by Ntotal, then sparsity s, with a small penalty for more total experts. They propose maximizing Ntotal and ntopk while minimizing nexp under the constraints. They report that (128,8) consistently beating (256,16) confirms this, and they acknowledge that validation at larger scale is needed.
record.recipe_differences: Studies MoE architecture and configuration scaling rather than reproducing the original dense-language-model scaling experiments; uses log-scale regression for a fixed-token sweep and a Chinchilla-style fit for two MoE configurations.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss changes with granularity and width-to-depth ratio. The fitted parameter and dataset exponents differ between the two tested MoE configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed Ntotal and sparsity, more total experts slightly raise loss (exponent +0.023 on nexp). The (128,8) configuration beats (256,16) at equal N and D.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE loss depends on expert count and sparsity beyond total or active parameter count.

record.problems: The authors report experiments only on small to medium models and datasets, limited architecture search and hyperparameter tuning, and the need for larger-scale validation. Random-seed uncertainty is reported for the architecture ablations, but uncertainty estimates for the fitted scaling-law coefficients are not stated. Some comparisons are shown only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results bearing on the claim were intentionally left out.

untested.parts: No compute sweep. The token range is only 9B–50B (about 5x), not several orders of magnitude. Parameter scaling spans roughly 2 orders of magnitude (30M–3B).
Not tested: no extrapolation from small runs to much larger ones.
Not tested: no compute-optimal N/D split is derived.
No fitting-method, schedule or data comparisons. No test of curvature away from a power law.

record.verdict_notes: r26–r31 are comparisons between alternative regression predictors, i.e. model selection. They bear on V1 only in that all of them fit well. No uncertainties are reported for the Chinchilla-style coefficients, and B=640,500 for (256,16) suggests a poorly constrained fit. The width-to-depth ablations used 4B tokens, and the parameter budgets are only approximately matched. The Qwen3-235B configuration derivation is an application, not a test.

versions.untested_parts: No compute-scaling sweep; token-budget scaling is tested only for two MoE configurations.
Does not show that fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Optimizes architecture under fixed memory and inference constraints, not the parameter/token split under a fixed compute budget.
Tests granularity and width-to-depth ratio in the explored configurations, not all architecture details or a general wide range of model sizes.
Uses text-pretraining objectives; does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Reports held-out language-model loss, not downstream-task performance.
Does not test compute-optimal splits, compare published laws directly, or report curves bending away from a single power law.
